stem: What does the course recommend doing with the ERP when deploying AI?

options.a: Replace it first with a new AI-native ERP platform
options.b: Keep it as system of record; add a thin layer on top
options.c: Freeze every change to the ERP until the AI project is live everywhere
options.d: Load all its data into the model's training set

explanation: Big-bang migrations delay value for years. Agents and apps sit on top of existing systems, read from them and write decisions back.
author: claude-spec

stem: Across more than 100 agentic deployments, roughly how much of the data agents need lives in no system of record?

options.a: Less than 5%
options.b: About 15%
options.c: About 40%
options.d: More than 80%

explanation: Much of the needed data sits in people's heads and in spreadsheets. Someone has to extract it on site, which is a large part of an FDE's job.
author: claude-spec

stem: A scheduling tool is configured from ERP routings and standard rates only. What is its most likely first failure?

options.a: Plans that ignore real constraints, which the floor then overrides
options.b: Reports that take far too long to load for the planners
options.c: Exposure of confidential salary data to everyone on the planning team
options.d: Licence costs that run well above the agreed budget

explanation: ERP master data is often wrong or incomplete: identical rates for different machines, missing family constraints. Plans built on it look valid on screen and fail on the floor.
author: claude-spec

stem: Two systems both claim to own machine status. What is the right design rule?

options.a: Average the two values every hour
options.b: Let the AI pick whichever value looks more plausible each time
options.c: Add a third system that reconciles both overnight
options.d: One owner system per field; other sources are copies

explanation: Each fact needs exactly one owner system. Two owners for the same fact is how a plant ends up with several OEE figures and no truth.
author: claude-spec

stem: A nightly data load crashes halfway and is rerun. Which property prevents duplicate records?

options.a: Higher parallelism across all of the load jobs
options.b: Idempotency, through stable keys and upserts
options.c: Compression of the intermediate files
options.d: A longer retention period for raw extracts

explanation: An idempotent pipeline gives the same result however many times it runs. Stable business keys and upserts make reruns safe.
author: claude-spec

stem: An AI agent decides tomorrow's production sequence. Where should that decision end up?

options.a: Written back into the existing systems people already work in
options.b: In a separate AI dashboard that planners can consult on the side when they wish
options.c: In a new database meant to replace the ERP over the coming years
options.d: In a report emailed to the plant manager every morning

explanation: The thin layer reads from existing systems and writes decisions back to them. A side dashboard or a parallel database leaves the real process untouched.
author: claude

stem: Your IT director says all the data an AI agent needs is already in your systems; only access is missing. What does the course say?

options.a: Correct: connecting the systems through APIs fully solves the data question for agents
options.b: Much of it lives in heads and spreadsheets and must be gathered on site
options.c: True for large plants, but rarely the case for small sites
options.d: Correct, provided the data is first moved to the cloud

explanation: Across more than 100 deployments, about 40% of the data agents need sat in no system of record. Access alone does not reach it; someone must extract it in the field.
author: claude

stem: A planner keeps a spreadsheet of which machines really can run which products. How should an AI project treat it?

options.a: As noise, since only ERP data counts as official company data
options.b: As shadow IT that should be shut down before the project starts
options.c: As a real data source to capture and bring into the model
options.d: As a temporary file to ignore until the ERP is updated

explanation: Spreadsheets and people's heads hold much of the data agents need. Ignoring or banning them throws away the rules that make plans feasible.
author: claude

stem: The first time AI runs on your plant data, it reveals many errors and gaps. How should leadership read this?

options.a: As proof that the vendor's tool is not working properly
options.b: As a clear sign the project should pause until all the data has been cleaned
options.c: As expected: data looks worse the day AI first runs on it
options.d: As a reason to replace the ERP before going any further

explanation: Data problems surface once AI uses the data, and that is normal. Budget for it rather than reading it as failure or as a reason to stop.
author: claude

stem: Your COO wants all plant data fully cleaned before any AI project starts. What does the course suggest?

options.a: Agree, since AI running on imperfect data produces worthless results
options.b: Start on one use case and fix the data it needs as you go
options.c: Set up a data team to clean every system over the next two years
options.d: Buy a tool that corrects all historical data automatically

explanation: Cleaning everything first delays value indefinitely and cleans data nobody uses. A use case shows which data matters, and that data gets fixed.
author: claude

stem: Before an AI agent is connected to company systems, who should decide what data it may see?

options.a: The AI vendor, based on what its tool needs to perform well
options.b: IT alone, since access is a technical configuration choice
options.c: The project team, which can open access as needs arise during the work
options.d: Business owners, setting who sees what and on which terms

explanation: Data access is a business decision. Who sees what, under which terms, is settled before connecting AI, not left to vendors or to configuration.
author: claude

stem: A vendor asks for full read access to your ERP to see what its AI can find. What is the right first step?

options.a: Decide who sees which data, on what terms, before connecting anything
options.b: Grant it, since read-only access cannot change or damage any data
options.c: Grant it for one month, then review what was accessed
options.d: Refuse all access until the AI has proven its value elsewhere

explanation: Read access still exposes data. The terms of access are a business decision to take before connecting; refusing everything blocks the work instead.
author: claude

stem: Your team needs the history of repairs and preventive work on each machine. Which system usually holds it?

options.a: The PLM
options.b: The WMS
options.c: The CMMS
options.d: The plant historian

explanation: The CMMS (computerized maintenance management system) records work orders, repairs and preventive maintenance. PLM holds product data, WMS the warehouse, APS the plan.
author: claude

stem: An agent needs real cycle times and machine signals from the line. Where do these usually come from?

options.a: SCADA systems and historians
options.b: The ERP's finance module
options.c: The PLM's product records
options.d: The ERP's routing and standard rate tables

explanation: SCADA and historians capture machine signals at the source. The ERP holds standard times, which often differ from what machines actually do.
author: claude

stem: An engineering change revises a product's drawings and specifications. Which system should own that revision?

options.a: The MES
options.b: The PLM
options.c: The WMS
options.d: The CMMS

explanation: PLM owns product data: drawings, specifications, revisions. Other systems receive copies of what PLM releases.
author: claude

stem: The written procedure says changeovers take 45 minutes; operators say they vary widely. What should the team model?

options.a: The documented 45 minutes, since it is the official standard
options.b: An average of the procedure and the operators' estimates
options.c: Whatever value the quality manager confirms in writing
options.d: Measured changeovers observed on the floor

explanation: The documented process and the real one diverge. Models built on the official figure produce plans the floor cannot follow.
author: claude

stem: ERP data shows every job starting on time, but operators book all starts at the end of their shift. What follows?

options.a: The timestamps record bookings, not when the work really started
options.b: The plant's schedule adherence is excellent and needs no further work
options.c: Operators should be disciplined for booking late
options.d: The ERP clock is wrong and must be resynchronized before any analysis

explanation: Data produced by the official process can mislead. Here it measures the booking routine, not the work, so it cannot train or judge a scheduler.
author: claude

stem: Why can a model built only from process documentation give wrong recommendations on the floor?

options.a: Process documents are usually too short and vague for any model to learn from
options.b: Documented and actual processes diverge, through workarounds and unwritten rules
options.c: Documentation is usually written by consultants rather than staff
options.d: Models need numeric machine data and handle text documents poorly

explanation: How work actually happens differs from the official description. The workarounds and unwritten rules are what makes the real process work.
author: claude

stem: The ERP lead time for a part is 10 days; the last 20 orders took 18 to 25 days. What should the planning model use?

options.a: The ERP value, since the ERP is the system of record
options.b: The ERP value plus a fixed one-day safety margin on every order
options.c: The shortest lead time recorded across those orders
options.d: Measured lead times, with the ERP value flagged for correction

explanation: ERP lead times and rates are often wrong. Plan on what actually happens and get the master data fixed at its source.
author: claude

stem: All five presses share one standard rate in the ERP, but two are older and slower. What will an AI scheduler using it do?

options.a: Leave the older presses underused, with idle time on them
options.b: Refuse to produce a plan until rates differ
options.c: Overload the slow presses with plans the floor cannot meet
options.d: Detect the slow presses itself and adjust their rates without help

explanation: A tool trusts its inputs. Identical rates for different machines make plans that look valid on screen and fail on the slower presses.
author: claude

stem: A dispatcher reassigns jobs at 2 pm using a dashboard fed by a nightly ERP batch. What is the problem?

options.a: The dashboard is too detailed for quick decisions
options.b: Decisions are based on yesterday's plant, not today's
options.c: Nightly batches overload the ERP during the day
options.d: The dispatcher should not be reassigning jobs at all during a shift

explanation: Information latency: a daily batch means deciding on yesterday's plant. Mid-shift decisions need data refreshed at the pace of the decision.
author: claude

stem: Which decision suffers most if its data refreshes only once a day?

options.a: Reassigning jobs after a machine breaks down mid-shift
options.b: Reviewing supplier prices at the end of each month
options.c: Setting next year's capacity and investment plan
options.d: Preparing the quarterly scrap report that goes to the board

explanation: Latency matters when the decision is fast. A breakdown changes the plant within the hour; monthly and yearly decisions tolerate daily data.
author: claude

stem: IT is wary of an AI project touching the ERP. What first step does the course recommend?

options.a: Escalate to the CEO so that IT's concerns are overruled quickly
options.b: Ask for full write access so the pilot can show real value
options.c: Start with read-only extracts, then earn APIs and write-back
options.d: Wait until IT has finished building its own data platform

explanation: The access ladder wins IT early: read-only extracts, then APIs, then write-back, each step earned by the one before.
author: claude

stem: A pilot runs on read-only extracts and users now want it to update ERP orders. What comes next?

options.a: Grant write access now, since the users are asking for it
options.b: Have users retype the suggestions into the ERP by hand, indefinitely
options.c: Replace that ERP module with the pilot's own database
options.d: Move to API access, then validated write-back once trust is earned

explanation: Each rung of the access ladder is earned. Write-back comes after reliable API reads, with validation, not on demand.
author: claude

stem: Your team plans to involve IT only after the pilot succeeds. What is the main risk?

options.a: IT claims the credit for the gains the project produces
options.b: System access stalls just when the project needs to scale
options.c: The pilot costs more because IT charges internal rates
options.d: IT insists on replacing the ERP before any rollout can start

explanation: IT holds the keys to every rung of the access ladder. Bringing it in late means the rollout waits for reviews that could have run in parallel.
author: claude

stem: In the ISA-95 model, at which level does the MES sit?

options.a: Level 1
options.b: Level 2
options.c: Level 3
options.d: Level 4

explanation: Levels 0 to 2 cover sensing and control, level 3 manufacturing operations (MES), level 4 business planning (ERP).
author: claude

stem: A team wants a planning agent to change machine setpoints directly on the PLCs. Why is this a poor design?

options.a: PLCs use industrial protocols that modern software cannot read
options.b: It bypasses the execution and control layers where safety is managed
options.c: Setpoints are owned by the ERP, so the change must be made in the ERP first
options.d: Agents can only connect to systems that offer a REST API

explanation: In ISA-95 terms, planning sits at levels 3 and 4. Acting directly on level 0 to 2 control skips the layers that manage execution and machine safety.
author: claude

stem: Machine signals arrive every second at levels 0 to 2; the ERP thinks in orders and days. What does this imply for integration?

options.a: Stream every raw signal straight into the ERP so that it holds the complete picture
options.b: Ignore machine signals, since the ERP holds the official counts
options.c: Keep the signals only in the agent's context window as they arrive
options.d: Turn signals into events such as stops and counts before business layers use them

explanation: ISA-95 levels work at different time scales. Signals are condensed into events (stops, counts, states) before level 3 and 4 systems consume them.
author: claude

stem: Mid-shift job reassignment needs current order status. Which integration pattern fits best?

options.a: A nightly file extract from the ERP
options.b: A weekly full copy of the ERP database to a separate server
options.c: API reads on demand, or events from a message queue
options.d: A planner exporting a spreadsheet every morning

explanation: The pattern follows the decision's pace. Files and replicas refreshed daily or weekly suit slow decisions; APIs and queues serve decisions taken within the hour.
author: claude

stem: Your agent will start writing confirmed schedules back to the MES. What must the write path include?

options.a: Validation before each write and an audit trail of every change
options.b: Direct inserts into the MES tables, which are faster than going through any API
options.c: A nightly batch that overwrites the whole MES schedule
options.d: Automatic retries until the MES accepts each record

explanation: Read first; write back with validation and an audit trail. Retrying until accepted or overwriting in bulk hides errors in a system of record.
author: claude

stem: A pilot needs ERP data in week one, but API access requires a security review. What is a sensible start?

options.a: Screen-scrape the ERP using a shared user account
options.b: Pause all work until the API review is complete
options.c: Ask IT for direct write access to the ERP database while the review runs
options.d: A scheduled read-only extract while the API review proceeds

explanation: File extracts are a legitimate first integration pattern. They let work start safely while the next rung, API access, is reviewed.
author: claude

stem: Machine stop events can come from a message queue or from polling the database every minute. What does the queue add?

options.a: It removes the need to validate the incoming data
options.b: Events arrive as they happen, without loading the source
options.c: It stores the full event history, so the plant historian can be retired
options.d: It lets the agent write back without human approval

explanation: A queue pushes events to consumers when they occur. Polling adds load on the source and delay, and neither pattern removes validation.
author: claude

stem: In the three-layer data census, which three layers do you inventory?

options.a: Raw, cleaned and aggregated data
options.b: Master data, transactional data and reference data
options.c: System data, spreadsheet data and data in heads
options.d: Plant, regional and group-level data

explanation: The census asks where each needed fact lives: in systems, in spreadsheets or only in people's heads. The last two layers are often the largest.
author: claude

stem: Your census finds the real changeover rules only in a senior planner's memory. What is the right next step?

options.a: Walk real cases with the planner and record the rules in a structured form
options.b: Leave them out of scope until someone documents them in the ERP
options.c: Use the ERP's standard changeover times as a proxy
options.d: Let the model infer them from historical schedules without the planner's input

explanation: Data in heads is extracted by sitting with the expert on real cases. ERP standards miss the rules, and history alone cannot tell rules from habits.
author: claude

stem: Why run the data census before committing to a delivery date?

options.a: It replaces the need for interviews with operators and planners
options.b: It tells IT which systems need upgrading before the project starts
options.c: It proves to finance that the baseline is reliable
options.d: The share of data outside systems drives the extraction effort

explanation: Data in spreadsheets and heads must be extracted by hand, which takes time. The census sizes that work before a date is promised.
author: claude

stem: A quality engineer's spreadsheet holds the only list of approved material substitutions. How should the pipeline treat it?

options.a: Copy it once at the start of the project and stop updating it
options.b: As a source with a named owner, a fixed format and checks on load
options.c: Ignore it, because only data held in systems can be trusted in production
options.d: Ask the engineer to email changes to the team when they remember

explanation: Spreadsheet data is real data. Give it an owner, a format and load checks so it can feed production like any other source.
author: claude

stem: The MES logs 2% downtime on a press, yet output is 20% below a rate verified on the floor. What should you suspect first?

options.a: Operators overstating the parts they produce
options.b: A rounding error in how the MES stores durations
options.c: Unlogged micro-stops and slow cycles
options.d: Scrap being counted twice in the output total

explanation: Short stops and slow cycles rarely reach the downtime log. Data archaeology compares logged events with what the floor actually shows.
author: claude

stem: Logs show 90-minute changeovers; the procedure takes 40. Interviews reveal routine maintenance during changeovers. What follows?

options.a: Maintenance is hidden in changeover time and must be separated
options.b: The procedure is wrong and should be rewritten as 90 minutes
options.c: Operators are slow at changeovers and need retraining
options.d: The logs are unreliable and should be dropped from the analysis

explanation: Maintenance hidden inside changeovers is classic data archaeology. Separating the two shows the true changeover time and the real maintenance load.
author: claude

stem: A press's stop log tags 60% of stops as 'other'. What is the best use of this data?

options.a: Model those stops as random noise in the capacity plan
options.b: Delete the 'other' stops so that the reason analysis stays clean
options.c: Rely only on the 40% of stops that have a reason
options.d: Treat it as a lead and observe stops on the floor

explanation: Poor logs point to where the real causes hide. Going to the floor recovers them; discarding or modeling them as noise loses the signal.
author: claude

stem: Why compare logged downtime with downtime observed on the floor before modeling capacity?

options.a: Observed downtime is usually exaggerated by operators
options.b: Logged downtime is often understated, which overstates capacity
options.c: The comparison is needed to calibrate the machine sensors on the line
options.d: Auditors require it before any model goes live

explanation: Logs miss micro-stops and mislabel events. A model fed logged downtime assumes capacity the plant does not have.
author: claude

stem: An orders table that usually loads 2 million rows loads 200,000 tonight. Which check stops this reaching users?

options.a: A schema check that the column names and types are unchanged
options.b: A longer timeout on the load job
options.c: A row-count check against expected volume
options.d: A file compression ratio alert

explanation: Checks at each stage, such as row counts, null rates and ranges, catch partial loads. A schema check passes because the columns are fine.
author: claude

stem: Your pipeline reloads the full order history every hour and keeps getting slower. What is the standard fix?

options.a: Incremental loads of changed rows, keyed on stable business keys
options.b: More frequent full reloads, so that each run has less new data to absorb
options.c: Dropping all history older than one month from the pipeline
options.d: Moving the same full reload to a larger server

explanation: Incremental loads with upserts on business keys process only what changed. Full reloads grow with history however often they run.
author: claude

stem: The ERP team renames a column and your agent silently receives nulls for a week. What would have prevented this?

options.a: Running the pipeline twice as often
options.b: Granting the agent write access to the ERP
options.c: Keeping every raw extract for a longer retention period before deletion
options.d: A data contract with the source team, plus null-rate checks

explanation: A data contract fixes what the source delivers and who announces changes. Null-rate checks catch breaks the contract missed, on the first run.
author: claude

stem: A temperature feed suddenly shows 1,500 °C for a process that runs at 200 °C. Which check should catch it?

options.a: A duplicate check on the record keys
options.b: A row-count check on the batch
options.c: A range check at ingestion that holds or flags the data
options.d: A freshness check that the latest timestamp is recent enough

explanation: Range checks catch values outside physical limits. Row counts and freshness would pass, because the data arrived complete and on time.
author: claude

stem: You join orders to order lines, then sum order value. The total is three times too high. Why?

options.a: The inner join silently dropped every order that had no order lines at all
options.b: Each order repeats once per line, so its value is counted per line
options.c: Order values are stored in the wrong currency
options.d: The sum function rounds every value upward

explanation: A join to a many side repeats the one side's columns. Sum order-level values before joining, or sum at line level.
author: claude

stem: You need every machine with its count of stops this week, including machines with no stops. Which join?

options.a: A left join from machines to stops
options.b: An inner join between machines and stops
options.c: An inner join from stops to machines
options.d: A cross join between machines and stops

explanation: A left join keeps every machine and counts zero where no stop matches. An inner join silently drops the machines with no stops.
author: claude

stem: An inner join between orders and the customer table drops 5% of orders. What is the most likely cause?

options.a: The customer table is too large for the join to finish
options.b: The orders are duplicated in the source system and removed by the join
options.c: The join should use a window function instead
options.d: Those orders carry customer IDs missing from the customer table

explanation: An inner join keeps only matching rows. Orphan keys, often from data entry or migration, vanish silently; a left join and a null check reveal them.
author: claude

stem: You need each machine's running seven-day average scrap rate. Which SQL feature fits best?

options.a: A GROUP BY on machine only
options.b: A DISTINCT on machine and day
options.c: A window function partitioned by machine, ordered by day
options.d: A self-join of every row to every other row in the table

explanation: Window functions compute running values per partition without collapsing rows. A GROUP BY on machine gives one figure for the whole period.
author: claude

stem: Average cycle time per product is computed as the average of daily averages. What is the problem?

options.a: Days with few parts weigh as much as busy days
options.b: Daily averages cannot be stored as decimal numbers
options.c: The result double counts parts made across midnight
options.d: The daily averages should have been summed instead

explanation: An unweighted average of averages ignores volume. Sum cycle time and parts over the whole period, then divide.
author: claude

stem: Two plants in different time zones send events in local time. What should the pipeline do?

options.a: Convert everything to the headquarters' local time
options.b: Keep each plant's local times and compare the plants hour by hour
options.c: Drop the time part and keep only the date of each event
options.d: Store timestamps in UTC and keep each source's time zone

explanation: UTC makes events comparable and safe across daylight saving changes; keeping the source zone lets you rebuild local shift views.
author: claude

stem: A capacity model gives every machine 24 hours a day, but the plant runs two shifts and stops on weekends. What is missing?

options.a: The machines' standard rates from the ERP
options.b: The shift calendar, which defines available hours
options.c: The OEE target set for each machine
options.d: The historian's raw signal feed

explanation: Available time comes from the shift calendar, holidays and planned stops. Without it, capacity is overstated by a large factor.
author: claude

stem: One system records resin in kilograms, another in 25 kg bags. What should the pipeline do?

options.a: Let each downstream user convert the units when needed
options.b: Convert to one unit explicitly, with the factor stored and tested
options.c: Keep the larger figure when the two systems disagree
options.d: Treat both figures as the same unit to keep things simple

explanation: Units of measure must be explicit. A stored, tested conversion factor avoids silent errors of 25 times in stock and consumption.
author: claude

stem: A complaint names a defective finished lot. What data shows which raw material lots went into it?

options.a: Lot genealogy linking consumed lots to produced lots
options.b: The bill of materials for the finished product
options.c: The supplier's certificate of analysis for each delivery
options.d: The production order's planned start and end dates

explanation: The bill of materials says what should be used; genealogy records which actual lots were consumed. Only genealogy supports a trace or a recall.
author: claude

stem: A night shift runs from 10 pm to 6 am, and output is grouped by calendar day. What goes wrong?

options.a: Output is counted twice in the weekly totals
options.b: The night shift's data cannot be stored by the MES
options.c: Day shifts appear less productive than they are
options.d: Each night shift's output splits across two days

explanation: Shift-based metrics need the shift calendar, not midnight boundaries. Splitting a shift across two days distorts per-shift and per-day figures.
author: claude

stem: Your agent sets confirmed due dates. The ERP owns that field and the APS holds a copy. Where should the agent write?

options.a: To the ERP, which then feeds the copy in the APS
options.b: To both systems at once, so that they stay aligned
options.c: To whichever system the planner happens to have open
options.d: To a new table the agent owns, read by both systems

explanation: Writes go to the owner system; copies refresh from it. Writing to two places creates two owners and, soon, two truths.
author: claude

stem: Users edit item weights in the WMS copy, which now disagrees with the ERP that owns them. What is the fix?

options.a: Sync the WMS edits back to overwrite the ERP every night
options.b: Let each system keep its own value for its own purposes
options.c: Make edits in the ERP and refresh the WMS copy from it
options.d: Average the two weights in a nightly reconciliation job

explanation: Every field has one owner; other sources are copies that never take edits. Syncing edits back makes the copy a second owner.
author: claude

stem: Your agent reads orders and writes schedule proposals. How should its service account be set up?

options.a: With administrator rights, to avoid access errors in production
options.b: With only the permissions those two tasks need
options.c: Under a named planner's login, so actions are traceable
options.d: As one shared account for all of the project's tools

explanation: Least privilege limits damage when something goes wrong. A dedicated, logged service account is traceable without borrowing a person's login.
author: claude

stem: A database password appears in the pipeline's code repository. What should be done?

options.a: Make the repository private so that outsiders cannot see it
options.b: Rename the variable so the password is harder to spot
options.c: Leave it, since only the project team can read the code
options.d: Rotate it and move secrets to a store outside the code

explanation: Secrets live outside code. Once exposed, a password is compromised, so it is rotated; hiding the repository leaves it in the history.
author: claude

stem: An agent's write-back changed 40 orders overnight and planners ask why. What should already exist?

options.a: A rollback script that reverts all changes made by the agent
options.b: A rule that the agent writes only during the day shift
options.c: An audit log of each action, its inputs and the account used
options.d: A weekly summary email sent to the planners by the team

explanation: Audit logs make every automated write explainable: what changed, on which inputs, under which account. Without them nobody can answer the planners.
author: claude
